overview:
It began as one of several small Turkish principalities that filled the vacuum left in western Anatolia by the collapse of Seljuk and Byzantine authority. Later tradition fixed the founding to about 1299 under a frontier chief named Osman, but that date is a symbolic marker rather than a documented one: not a single written document survives from Osman's reign, and the Ottomans did not begin writing their own history until the fifteenth century, more than a hundred years after the events described. What followed is better attested. Ottoman forces crossed into Europe in the mid-fourteenth century and took much of the Balkans; Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire and giving the dynasty a capital that had been the pivot of the eastern Mediterranean for a millennium. Selim I's defeat of the Mamluks in 1516–17 brought Syria, Egypt and the guardianship of Mecca and Medina under Ottoman control, and under Suleiman, who ruled from 1520 to 1566, the empire took Belgrade, broke the Hungarian kingdom at Mohács in 1526, and reached the walls of Vienna in 1529.

At its greatest extent it stretched from Hungary and the Black Sea steppe through Anatolia and the Levant to Egypt, Iraq and the North African coast, holding together Turks, Greeks, Slavs, Arabs, Armenians, Kurds, Jews and many others. It governed that mixture through a sultan's household staffed in part by the devshirme, the levy of Christian boys who were converted, trained and set to serve as soldiers and administrators, and through a broad practice of leaving religious communities to run their own family law, schools and internal disputes in exchange for loyalty and taxes. That arrangement is usually called the millet system, though historians now caution that the tidy three-millet structure of Greek Orthodox, Armenian and Jewish communities was formalized only in the nineteenth century and then presented as ancient custom.

The older story of a long slide after 1566 has been largely abandoned; the empire remained a major power well into the eighteenth century. But the failed siege of Vienna in 1683 and the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 marked the beginning of sustained territorial loss, and the nineteenth century brought a running contest between reform and dismemberment — the Tanzimat decrees from 1839, a short-lived constitution in 1876, nationalist secessions in the Balkans, and European creditors and armies pressing from every side. The Young Turk revolution of 1908 restored constitutional rule; the empire entered the First World War alongside Germany, carried out the genocide of its Armenian population, lost its Arab provinces, and signed an armistice in 1918. The Turkish national movement that emerged from the wreckage abolished the sultanate on 1 November 1922.
significance: For six centuries the Ottomans held the hinge between Europe, Asia and Africa, controlling the land routes and much of the sea traffic that connected them, and their presence shaped European politics from the Habsburg frontier wars to the alliances that produced the First World War. They preserved and remade Constantinople as Istanbul, sustained an Islamic imperial culture of law, architecture and administration that outlasted its Persian and Mughal contemporaries, and governed religious plurality in ways that later states in the region both inherited and repudiated. The borders drawn in the empire's collapse — in Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Palestine, the Balkans and the Caucasus — remain among the most contested in the world, and the unresolved question of the Armenian genocide is still a live matter of state.
coverage: This was written from general reference works rather than specialist scholarship, and the dataset holds no events for the story at all, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped point. The deepest gap is in the record itself: the fourteenth-century origins rest entirely on chronicles written a century or more later, so the 1299 start date, Osman's ancestry and the order of his conquests are all disputed, and the once-standard reading of the early Ottomans as holy warriors has been substantially revised. Much of the surviving evidence for the later empire is administrative and state-produced, which means peasants, women, slaves and the empire's non-Muslim subjects are seen mostly through the paperwork of the people taxing or governing them.
